utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There is one preliminary but so short that we could already ask the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. It is about D01060. The translation which was provided by the Prosecution has now been uploaded by the Defence, and therefore it seems that the English translation was uploaded into e-court under doc ID number 1D19-2264 can be attached to D01060, and D1060 is admitted into evidence. I do understand, Mr. Traldi, that there was still some puzzles in relation to the transcription of the interview of the witness but that you'll further sort that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I've spoken with Mr. Lukic and we're in agreement as to how to proceed. Just briefly for the Chamber, essentially the transcript is correct as to the original words spoken in both languages, so the English translation was essentially correct for the English -- sorry, the English transcript. The B/C/S transcript essentially correct for the B/C/S. We've had it reviewed, and what I intend to do is simply pull up the relevant page of the reviewed version in B/C/S, ask the witness to read it for the record, and ask if he confirms it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems to be a very practical way of resolving the matter. Something apparently has gone wrong then in translation or the transcription of the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sokanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony. And Mr. Traldi will now continue his cross-examination. Please carefully listen to the question and try to answer them as directly as possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 32563A, page 55, in the B/C/S only.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And as it comes up, good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dobro jutro [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a portion of the transcript of your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor that we looked at yesterday. We've had it reviewed overnight, and what I'm going to ask to you do is simply begin at line 20, read the reviewed version of your answer slowly into the record, and then at the end tell us if you confirm the truthfulness and accuracy of what you've read. Beginning at line 20 with your initials and the words "ovi organi."

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "These organs were following the media, information media of the enemy, and our information about the enemy were published by the media. This organ, or this section, was in charge to the extent possible to monitor the Muslim/Croat media and to listen -- stations and to listen what they were broadcasting also to listen to the stations in Republika Srpska to see what they were broadcasting."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And do you confirm the truthfulness and accuracy of that answer?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So the record is clear, the organ or the sector that we're speaking of is the Main Staff's sector for legal, moral, and religious affairs; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The discussion here is about the information sector and the text says: "This organ," in line 3, "This organ, or department, was entrusted to the extent possible," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The information section, which staff sector in the Main Staff was that part of?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That section was one of the sections in the sector for morale, legal, and religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 32646.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, these are instructions issued by General Gvero dated the 9th of March, 1993. Below point 1, on the first page in both languages, we read about the presentation of what he describes as anti-Serbian propaganda in other countries. And turning to page 2 in the English in the first full paragraph, so the paragraph immediately above the Roman numeral II, and at the bottom of page 1, and top of page 2 in B/C/S, we read his evaluation that: "In other countries every citizen can see this for themselves on a daily basis on their TV screens or hear it from their radios or read it in the newspapers and magazines." Now this reflects that General Gvero was aware as of March 1993 that foreign media was reporting that serious crimes had been committed by Bosnian Serb forces. Yes?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the text in front of me is very illegible. I didn't manage to find the paragraph that you have just read to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I had some concerns there as well, Mr. Traldi. Could you, first of all, could we try to have the -- to have it enlarged to the extent possible for the witness. Even if need be, only the B/C/S on the screen so that it can be further enlarged. And second, could you then slowly read it again, the portion that you had in your mind. We'll try to make it better legible for you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now can you see at the very top of the page here a reference from General Gvero to the fact that every citizen can see this for themselves on a daily basis on their TV screens or hear it from their radios or read it in their newspapers and magazines; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, if we could scroll down to the middle of page 2 in the B/C/S, just to make clear that they are able to read that he's aware of to read and see and hear. In the middle of the page as we have it now, General Gvero refers to specific allegations: Aggression, ethnic cleansing, crimes, obstruction of humanitarian aid, and other activities. As of this point, early March 1993, it's clear that he was aware that such allegations were being made in the international press; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I cannot say what General Gvero knew or didn't know. Specifically it states here that those carrying out an anti-Serb campaign will attempt - attempt - among other things to find arguments in our media, to charge Serbs and their army for ethnic cleansing crimes, interfering with the delivery of humanitarian aid, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the witness very well, the interpreters note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are speaking away from the microphone. Can the microphone be adjusted. The usher will assist you. The interpreters have difficulties in hearing you. Could you resume your answer. You said: "... among other things to find arguments in our media, to charge Serbs and their army for ethnic cleansing crimes, interfering with the delivery of humanitarian aid, and so on and so forth." Was that the last part of your answer, or did you say anything after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you said you can't say what General Gvero knew or didn't know. At this point, the 9th of March 1993, he was your immediate superior; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: How often would you meet?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes we met on a daily basis, several times, and then at other times, we wouldn't see each other for a whole month.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: His office was about 30 metres away from yours? Or the building his office was in was about 30 metres away from the building your office was in?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what we're reading about here, information about the war, information about the actions of Bosnian Serb forces in the media, that was part of his job, part of your job, part of the responsibilities of the sector he ran and in which you worked; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. We exactly do not see it here as this gentleman said. This document says in English and it's the same in Serbian: Among other things, the campaigners -- the anti-Serbian sentiment will try. We do not see what happened, what -- it's his what -- assumption of General Gvero what somebody will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Is it Mr. Lukic's case that there'd been no reports of such crimes before this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm discussing this document that is in front of this witness. There are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to clearly separate the objection against the question and what Mr. Lukic's case is. These are two different matters. At the same time, could you -- in your question, could you phrase it again Mr. Traldi, and could you avoid anything that could be possibly understood as not quoting correctly the text before us, and then of course you can put whatever question you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Coverage and potential coverage of the war and of the actions of the VRS was part of General Gvero's responsibilities, part of your responsibilities, and part of the responsibilities of your sector, his sector in the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was part of the responsibilities of the chief of the sector, i.e., General Gvero, and the section for information in the sector for morale, religious, and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So what I'm putting to you is your testimony that you can't say what General Gvero knew about international coverage of the actions of the VRS at that time is not the truth. That you, at the time, were aware that he was aware of the nature and the tone of international coverage of the regular allegations of crimes by Bosnian Serb forces, including the VRS. That's the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Below that, General Gvero writes about particularly sensitive information that at the time is coming out the Eastern Bosnia and suggests that this information should be carefully monitored. That's because the Main Staff was capable of monitoring the information coming out of Eastern Bosnia at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff received information from subordinate units and commands, including those that were located in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In fact, by this time, the Main Staff's sector for legal, moral, and religious affairs was putting out daily reports on what it termed Muslim and Croat propaganda; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they were not doing it at that time. I think we're talking about early 1993 here. But during a certain period, yes. I cannot remember the time-period though in which they did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, we may have occasion to look at one or two later and see if we can refresh your recollection. But for the moment, this time, March of 1993 in Eastern Bosnia, one of the things that happened was the enclave of Cerska fell; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was when Cerska was liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the people living in Cerska, the Muslims who had been there, they fled when it was, as you say, liberated; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so, but I wasn't there. According to my information, though, they did leave that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And there was a humanitarian crisis in March 1993 in the Srebrenica enclave; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have information about whether there was a humanitarian crisis or not. But in any case, a large number of people arrived in the area, and the living conditions then were not the same as they were before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you say "not the same," they were very bad, the living conditions; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so. I really cannot say because I didn't have the opportunity to see so for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you testified yesterday that the Main Staff's position was that journalists could write freely and move freely. We read here that in the context of the events we just discussed, General Gvero's position is: "All uncontrolled and unorganised movements of the local and foreign journalists in the theatre of war must be prevented." This is an example of General Gvero applying a more restrictive policy than the one you described yesterday; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I do see the paragraph. I see what you have just read out to me. In general the position of the Main Staff, which sent instructions to the units, was that domestic and foreign journalists for their personal safety should not be permitted or permitted extremely rarely to move about the combat zone. Naturally, journalists could not move around unless they were accredited in the proper way by the Ministry of Information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we decide on that -- Witness, the conditions or the limitations on the free movement here, as far as can I read, have got nothing to do with safety but are about a risk of propaganda or misinformation. Would you agree with that? Because I don't see any reference to safety. I see it's embedded in a document which deals with anti-Serb propaganda.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecutor put this question to me right after several questions that had to do with the Cerska operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I think the Prosecutor was asking the sensitivity of the information, and he wanted to find out what that was. But I'm now putting the question to you whether you agree that the context of this document is not one that refers to safety and security of the journalists but which is about a risk of publications which are anti-Serb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you could interpret it in that way, but you could interpret it also in a different way. On the basis of this text, it's difficult to see what it's all about. I think that in the specific instance there should have been no danger from this information being released in view of the fact that the UNPROFOR commander, General Morillon, happened to be in Srebrenica at that time himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, what I read in this document - and there may have been some confusion in the questions put by Mr. Traldi as well - is that there is concern about the information which is provided by the Serbs themselves is used for arguments so as to accuse the Serbs from all kind of things. That's the context of this document. And, Mr. Traldi, I'm saying that it may not have always been very clear because information in your questions it's not always clear whether you refer to information coming from the Serbs, as we find clearly on the bottom of the previous page and then the top of this page, and then the information you can read in the media which, of course, is something different. But that's the context, Witness, isn't it? Abuse of your information for accusing the Serbs of all kind of things, that's the context. Do you agree or do you not agree; and, if not, and if you think it's more about safety, please point at where specifically safety and security is referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this part of the text in front of me, I don't see anywhere that the safety of journalists is discussed. It also says that we particularly believe the information from the area to be sensitive, and the position of the Main Staff, and it regulated this through instructions, that the information should be issued regularly in an objective way and in a timely way. That it should be truthful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did that already. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 32646 receives number P7392, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7392 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have P6646.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a document dated the 19th of November, 1994, entitled: "Directions on Some Current Issues Regarding Public Information." And it's sent to the assistant commanders for moral guidance, religious, and legal affairs of the various corps, the various logistics bases, and several other units. Those are all units, corps, and logistics bases directly under -- directly subordinated to the VRS Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is your document; right? You produced it.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, but I cannot see the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let's turn to the end for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see that. I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And this document sets out generally how VRS units are to behave in terms of public information, what information to provide; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. I didn't manage to read the entire document. That is one of the guide-lines that we sent out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Is this a document you would have produced on your own authority or would one of your superiors have had to approve it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have authority of my own. Whenever General Gvero was present, if I wrote anything, I wrote it on his orders and with his approval, or if somebody else wrote it, then I would sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So General Gvero would have approved this document being disseminated; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have page 2 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm directing your attention to point 12 which we already see in front of you in the B/C/S. We read that this part of the document, you direct those units: "Mask our offensive activities maximally. Do not inform the public about these, but in the advanced stage, present them as ... the natural right to self-defence and a forced response, in other words, a counteroffensive." You are directing that the public be intentionally misled about the VRS's offensive operations; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please speak directly into the microphone, not on the side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you try to speak directly into the microphone. And it could perhaps be adjusted again. Perhaps you sit slightly back or that it ... Yes, we're not blaming you for anything, but we try to hear the words you are speaking. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for these difficulties. I don't know whether you can hear me properly now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you now please answer the question whether you were intentionally instructed to mislead the public about offensive activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in any war, all conflicting armies try up to a maximum to conceal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one yet asked whether it's justified or whether there were good reasons to do that. The question simply is whether you instructed that the public should be misled intentionally about offensive activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we gave instructions to mask activities to a maximum degree so that they would remain secret so that they do not be made public.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And we didn't hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the end of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At a later stage, it should be portrayed as a counteroffensive. If that's what I said at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, what I'm putting to you is that aside from masking the operations, separate from any attempt to keep them secret, what you're suggesting is that offensive activities should be presented as part of self-defence or as counteroffensives as a forced response rather than the offensive activities that you're saying in this document that they were. That is an instruction to mislead the public; right? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely as written here, Your Honours and Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That is precisely yes, it is an instruction to mislead the public; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why we would have any reason to deceive our public in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: One reason that you intended -- one reason you issued this order to deceive the public in the -- at home and abroad, was you knew the offensive activities of the VRS were controversial and prompted international criticism; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot give an answer because I'm not aware of such criticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your evidence today, as you sit there, is you're aware of no international criticism of the VRS during the war for its offensive activities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in this stage - so in this stage - I really cannot recall that we had this information. I personally did not have any information pertaining to the international public. I state that with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you recall as you sit there any international criticism of the VRS or the Bosnian Serbs at all?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall individually some of these pieces of information that were written up via the information department on the basis of listening to the radio of Republika Srpska in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some part where this criticism was being conveyed, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: How about coverage of the camps right around when you joined the Main Staff? Do you recall international criticism of conditions in the camps run by the VRS and other Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in relation to that I do remember because precisely a day or two or three - I cannot remember exactly right now - after I arrived in the Main Staff and joined the Army of Republika Srpska, I was sent to report to the president of Republika Srpska in Pale so that he could issue concrete orders to me and that on behalf of the army I should accompany the ICRC and foreign journalists when they visit prisons for prisoners of war. I think that that was after one of the peace conferences. And I carried out that mission; I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Which camps did you visit?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first day we visited -- it was towards the end of the day, actually. We visited the prison of Kula in Sarajevo. That is in the area that is nowadays called east Sarajevo. Then the next day, we visited Keraterm, Trnopolje, and another prison, but I really cannot recall the name. Perhaps if you could jog my memory. I certainly wouldn't mind. But at any rate, it was those three. What was proposed was that the prison in Batkovic and in Batkovici -- Bijeljina too and also the one in Manjaca be visited, but people from this convoy were not interested in visiting these prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You said you can't recall the name of the third prison. Would it refresh your recollection if I said Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So at the beginning of your time in the Main Staff, you visited Omarska, Keraterm, Trnopolje, among other camps run by the Bosnian Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received a great deal of evidence about these visits. Earlier -- so I'm not going to go through them in detail. But earlier I asked whether you recalled any international criticism of the VRS or the Bosnian Serbs at all. You said you recalled some pieces of information written up via the information department. Now, in fact, there was an enormous amount of international condemnation of the conditions in the camps that you visited together with these journalists as a representative of the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a member of the Main Staff who was not assigned a particular duty until then. I want to say that these three camps that you mentioned, with the exception of Kula, were under the control of - what was it called then? - the Ministry of Interior something, the centre of public security, and so on and so forth. The prison in Kula was under the control of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And there had been preparations made by subordinate units directed by the Main Staff to get the camps ready for these visits; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I don't know, but of course there was a representative of the government and a representative of the Ministry of Interior there, along with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You said you were sent to President Karadzic. Did you have any discussions with other Main Staff officers about what was being done to get ready for these visits or about what you would be likely to see on these visits?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a brief issuing of an order by General Gvero. It was a spoken order. I was supposed to report to the president of the republic urgently, and I was supposed to take journalists and members of the ICRC around, and all other instructions I will get from the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 31356.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is an order issued by Colonel Dragan Ilic, at the time the commander of the East Bosnia Corps to the POW camp commander. We see it's dated the 3rd of August, 1992. That's around the time of your visit; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe a day after the visit or the day when the visit was supposed to take place. I quite simply cannot recall the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, he is directing that prisoners over the age of 70 be released. Were you aware at the time of your visit that the VRS was detaining prisoners over the age of 70 in its camps?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the Kula prison and I don't think I saw any elderly persons there as prisoners. It's not that I think so; I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to ask again for an answer to my question. Were you aware at the time of your visit that the VRS was detaining prisoners over the age of 70 in its camps? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Detaining elderly people, people who visibly appeared to be non-combatants, that's the sort of thing that would prompt the sort of international condemnation that came as a result of the visits to and coverage of the camps; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would only be natural to expect that kind of condemnation. I cannot give you an answer to that question because this was written by the commander of the Eastern Bosnia Corps, and I repeat once again that I am more and more certain that we travelled on the second; that is, Saint Ilijas day. That's when we were in Kula. And on the 3rd we were in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to move on. Before I do, I'll tender this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31356 receives number P7393.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7393 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did Colonel Ilic later acquire a position in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He became the chief of the sector for operations; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What position did he get?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He became the head of the operations organ in the staff. The operative staff of the Main Staff, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have P2879.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is an order issued by General Mladic dated the 3rd of August, 1992. See it's sent to the commander personally. It says: "Pursuant to the agreement of political leadership of three BiH peoples, reached at the recent negotiations in London and in goal of preparation of the POW camps for visits and making possible for foreign journalists and members of the International Committee of the Red Cross to visit them." He issues an order, first to: "... undertake measures through the MUP and authorities to arrange POW camps in your zones of responsibility and prepare them for visits by foreign journalists and the International Committee of the Red Cross team." This the visit you took part in; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Looking at point 3, he notes: "You will be additionally informed on the precise time of the visit to POW camps. The tour started 3 August 1992 in the zone of responsibility of Sarajevo-Romanija Corps." Does that refresh your recollection as to the date of your visit to Kula?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you were aware in the late summer/early fall of 1992, you and the morale sector yourself were aware that the VRS was detaining people it had no legal basis to detain; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything for sure because the organ for morale and religious affairs to deal with prisons and POWs. Sometimes some information would arrive as an indicator or factor that affected combat morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that information that would sometimes arrive as a factor that affected combat morale was that the VRS was detaining people it had no legal basis to detain; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, or I'm not aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, we had a few incidents yesterday about speaking aloud. I gave you a last warning. I repeat that now and next time will result in consequences. Please proceed. And, Witness, Mr. Sokanovic, you just focus on Mr. Traldi who is examining you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have P3951.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a 1st Krajina Corps combat morale report for August 1992 dated the 3rd of September. General Gvero would have reviewed this report personally and shared the contents with General Mladic and the collegium; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reviewed -- or, rather, he reviewed that. Now, he was supposed to communicate that if he thought it was of significance, but that does not necessarily mean that he did communicate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to the page 3 in the English and to page 4 in the B/C/S under the category "The Effect of the Political and Security Situation in the Territory on Combat Morale," so at the very bottom of the page in the English, we read that the 1st Krajina Corps is reporting: "Certain tensions are still present in the Kotor Varos, Kljuc, Sanski Most and Prijedor areas," and we haven't scrolled quite far enough down in the English yet, "because of a large number of arrested citizens for whom there is no evidence or criminal reports that they participated in the armed rebellion." So General Gvero by this point -- at this point, 3rd of September 1992, he's being informed by a subordinate corps that a large number of people have been arrested with no legal basis; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what is written here, but it doesn't say who it was that took them prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The Chamber has received evidence that by this time most of them were being detained at Manjaca, including some who'd been transferred from facilities run by the police. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was well known that the prison of Manjaca existed; however, in this case, as can be seen from this text, it says here that the centre of security services contributes to this situation headed by Drljaca. And yesterday we discussed this. At the time, there were many paramilitary formations that were prominent precisely in these places.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I understand you're attempting to focus on the public security station. At this point, my question is: Were you aware that these people who'd been arrested and detained with no legal basis were being detained at the VRS-run Manjaca camp, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is time for the break. Witness we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, could you inform the Chamber whether you're on track as far as time is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I am. And I should say that's based on what I've been informed, which is that have I about 45 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Assuming that, as usual, Madam Registrar is correct in that regard, then I'm on track.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the information is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may continue, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You mentioned one of the places you visited was Kula. I have a couple of questions for you about it. First, was Radovan Karadzic on the same visit to Kula you went on?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Are you aware of coverage in the international press of him handing out a small number of discharge certificates on a visit to Kula in early August 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received evidence that 10.000 or more civilians passed through Kula, were detained there, were eventually exchanged during the war. Is it your evidence that you don't know anything about that either?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The Chamber has also received evidence that days after your visit to Omarska, the prisoners from Omarska were transferred to Manjaca and that the people who were transferred included minors, people who were elderly, people who were ill, people who, in the view of the Manjaca guards, couldn't hold a gun let alone run or shoot. Did you see people like that on your visit to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went to Omarska, I did not attend any talks, but I did have the opportunity to see some prisoners, among whom were people who were, I would say, first of all, of a weak physical constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: People who looked like they hadn't been getting enough food; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You saw people who looked like they hadn't been getting enough food on your visit to Trnopolje too; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in a position to see how much food they were getting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You were in a position to see them. They looked, they were of a very weak, very thin physical constitution. In your words, they looked like they hadn't been getting enough food; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Individually, yes, but not all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the Chamber has received evidence that some of the ones who looked that way had been transferred from Keraterm where you said you visited. Were you aware, as the Chamber has received evidence, the Main Staff was that a large number of prisoners had been killed at Keraterm just about ten days earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was patient enough. I object to this type of questions, that the Chamber received the evidence. Is that question for this witness? Should he comment on that, what chamber received? Or should he answer anything when Chamber received evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think it's reminding the witness. But, Mr. Traldi, if you want to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As Mr. Lukic I thought said, but perhaps did not, the same objection has been raised and ruled on by the Chamber before, I think, in the context of Witness Dragojevic's testimony. It's a practice that we've followed throughout the Defence case and Mr. Lukic has objected a couple of times recently, but I think it's fair for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If there is an evidence that -- this evidence should be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that's not necessary. I -- unfortunately, you don't understand in that respect. What you do is you tell the witness that the Chamber is not blank on these matters but that we have received information about it. Whether that's convincing or not, whether that establishes facts or not, the question is not to comment on that evidence. The question is: Are you aware that a large number of persons were killed ten days before that, an event on which this Chamber has received some evidence. Now, the knowledge of the witness does not depend on the evidence this Chamber receives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why mention the evidence then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you could do without, and then in the next question -- but in itself it's not improper to tell the witness that this Chamber is not blank in this field, that we have received evidence, whatever that evidence is. That's my ruling. The witness may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Moloto who is educated, I would say, in the system, would like to add something to my ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The purpose for telling the witness the evidence is to give the witness an opportunity to either confirm or deny that evidence, and if he does confirm then you can follow -- you can close the question, but if he does deny you can follow up to find out on what basis. That's the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. But I informed this Chamber that many of my witnesses complained that it is very confusing to them. They don't know what to do if with that type of question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's unfortunate if they are confused but that's the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could have explained it then what the situation is as I explained it a minute ago to you, Mr. Lukic. The objection is denied. Witness, were you aware that some ten days before a large number of people were killed in Keraterm? And again, this Chamber -- again, this Chamber is not blank on the matter. We have received evidence related to such an event.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've already answered the Prosecutor's question. I did not have any knowledge about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We did not hear the last few words of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last few words. You said you didn't have any knowledge about ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About ten days before the International Red Cross arrived and the international journalists whom I accompanied, that any killings of people were committed who were in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, that massacre was included in a daily combat report to the Main Staff. Is it your evidence that nobody at the Main Staff said, "Okay, you're going to Keraterm. You should know people were killed. You should know it's a recent massacre site." Nobody briefed you about that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct. Nobody told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Were the journalists taken to room 3 at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't even know what room 3 is, and I cannot recall any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did you go by a room with bullet-holes in the door?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not notice anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you didn't take them into a room where there were still traces of blood, traces of an execution?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it established that at the time when this gentleman was there there were traces of killings still?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that's suggested in the question and the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, did you take them to the room where there were traces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To a room, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To a room --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- where traces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- where there were traces. That's a perfectly permissible question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But we don't know whether there were traces at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the witness will tell us what he knows, and there's a suggestion that there was a room with traces of blood. Now, the witness can either confirm or deny that. It's not that it should be established. By the way, this Chamber has not established any facts at this moment about these matters. We do that at the end. We do it in our judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, but we received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the objection is denied. We'll continue. Did you take them to a room in which there was traces of blood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not see traces of blood in any room or in any facility. I don't know which room they were taken to because in that part -- or actually, in all of those prisons, the team was led by a member of the public security centre from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You yourself were not present in those rooms, if I understand you well? In what, as you called them, prisons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, I was not present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I just have a couple of more questions on this topic, sir. First, when you say "those three prisons," you mean Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje; right.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And I apologise. In my previous answer to Mr. President, the Presiding Judge, not that I was not in any of the rooms. I was in a restaurant, or the canteen, and I was in the office of the prison warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's at Omarska; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I may have been confused by not knowing exactly what prison or prisons the witness was talking about. Could you -- if you say anything about either Keraterm or Trnopolje or Omarska to make clear which of those facilities you are referring to. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you said you saw people who didn't -- who appeared they didn't have enough food, people appeared in a weak physical condition. Did you tell General Gvero about that when you got back to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned to Pale, I drafted a report that I submitted to the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And did you also tell your superior?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed him about what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it would have been his responsibility to inform General Mladic, inform the collegium of the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it should have been, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And there were people wearing military uniforms as guards, at least at Trnopolje; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes. It's an area around the school and some construction material warehouse that was fenced in with a wire fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And around that area, people wearing VRS uniforms serving as guards; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period, the police and the army wore mostly camouflage uniforms. In some situations, the police also had blue uniforms as well as the camouflage uniforms. I think, even though I cannot remember right now, that they had camouflage uniforms; although, I cannot really state that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you're aware the VRS did external security at Omarska; right? The VRS was responsible for external security at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- I don't know that. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Are you aware of any measures that your superior, General Gvero, or anyone else on the Main Staff took after this visit to investigate, for instance, the Prijedor Brigade commanders related to the VRS's involvement in those camps?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if this happened. What I do know is that when we were received by the Prijedor public security service -- centre chief, I learned that those three prisoners [as interpreted] were under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you say "those three prisoners," or did you say "those three prisons"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those three prisons, Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now the Chamber has received a great deal of evidence about Slobodan Kuruzovic who at the time was in charge of Trnopolje. Do you recall if you met him?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I'm hearing the name for the first time so that I cannot really say if I met him or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did you meet the warden at Trnopolje? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He was wearing a green camouflage uniform; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps, but I'm finding it difficult to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to move away from Prijedor now. In fact, the VRS continued detained civilians into 1993 and longer; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, or I just cannot remember that at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have P6915.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As it comes up, this is going to be an order by General Milovanovic dated the 24th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the document is P6915.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it 6915 or 6195.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: 6915. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, we see here, and we don't have the B/C/S, but it's an order General Milovanovic is issuing to the various corps and the air force and anti-aircraft defence to provide details of prisoners to the Main Staff with the aim of conducting talks on the exchange of prisoners of war and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if we could have page 2 in the English only, and it's the end of the text in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He's directing that lists be provided of "Muslim prisoners of war and captured civilians in prisons of the RS." Is it your evidence that you, though you were in the Main Staff at the time, were not aware that there were captured civilians, captured Muslim civilians, in RS prisons?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received a number of lists of prisoners kept by subordinate units - for instance, P6804, P6805, and P7239 - that reflected, among others, the detention of 100-year-old Muslim women. So I'd put to you that it's clear from this document the Main Staff was aware and that you are testifying today that are you not aware of civilians being detained because you know it to have been unlawful. That's the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm just one of the members of the Main Staff, and in a sector that as for POW camps, their keeping, their exchanges -- or rather exchanges of prisoners, we had nothing do with that. I had nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No corps commanders or corps assistant commanders for security and intelligence were dismissed after the publicity about the terrible criminal conditions in the camps, were they?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, not a single one was dismissed. And I assume, as far as the content of their work is concerned, there were other omissions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And no guards were sentenced to terms of imprisonment in the VRS military justice system, were they?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In one of the lists of prisoners that contained elderly people and Muslim civilians that I referred to, P7239, was the TG Visegrad list. At the time, its commander was Dragisa Masal. He was also promoted to serve at the Main Staff afterwards; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what year that was. I don't know from what year that report is. General Dragisa Masal was then a colonel. He was not promoted. He was transferred from that position to another position in the Main Staff. The actual transfer did not mean that it was any kind of reward.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you have more authority as chief of artillery in the Main Staff or as the commander of TG Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it depends on the area involved. The commander of the tactical group is the commander and he is sovereign, if I can put it that way, in terms of the unit or units that he commands. And the chief of a certain service is primarily in charge of the professional management of that particular service in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, we've been talking about the detention of civilians. Your view in your interview was that on all three sides people were reluctant to talk about civilian victims and often described them as soldiers; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's -- in your view, then, it was wasn't popular to make known that there were civilian victims of the acts of the VRS or any of the other parties to the conflict; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was popular, as you had put it. I would kindly ask you, if it's not a problem, to remind me of that particular part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 32563, page 43 in the English and 54 in the B/C/S. And, actually, let's have 32563a but the same pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we see you're asked: "What would happen if a crime against a large number of civilians was committed? Would that case be handed over to the security department?" You say: "Yes, I'm not sure whether directly to the security department or directly to the prosecutor. Anyway, it had to be investigated and then the measures undertaken. You have to be aware that all three sides almost never spoke or very rarely spoke about, you know, the civilian victims. Unfortunately, that's the reality. So usually everyone was, you know, treated, referred to as the soldiers." And you say: "Sometimes that was right because soldiers throw away their weapons." And you add that: "Everyone knew the civilians were protected by the Geneva Conventions." First, do you stand by your answer in your interview that I've just described?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely the last sentence that you read out confirms that. Because people, I mean, were portrayed as civilians and they were combatants in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, you're focusing on a different part of your answer. What you say in the beginning of the answer is that civilians would be described as soldiers, all three sides almost never spoke about civilian victims, and everyone was treated and referred to as soldiers. First, do you stand by that portion of your answer?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to find it now. It's at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Should be the third, fourth, and fifth sentences.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm counting the sentences now, and the third one says: "Unfortunately, that is reality. And all were mostly treated as combatants. Sometimes that was done rightly because when somebody would get into a bad situation, they knew they would fair better if they threw away their rifles and presented themselves as civilians." And then further on, there is the part that refers to protection by the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And now please read the sentence before the word "unfortunately."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, it says: "You should know that all three sides almost never spoke about civilian victims, and if so, very little. Everyone was treated and referred to as soldiers." This pertains to statements made to the media. And, of course, such statements would disturb the public, and I presume that that is the reason why that didn't -- that -- that there was no wish to show it that way, as victims in that area. Civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And now listen to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: First, can I take it you stand by that portion of your answer as truthful and accurate? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the sense in which I spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Second, you've been doing the same thing this morning, denying knowledge of civilian victims, because you know they're entitled to legal protection because it could be disturbing, the same thing you did during the war; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't actually understand your question. Please, could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sure. Let me break it up. First, the statements made to the media that you said -- in which you said everyone was treated or referred to as soldiers, those were made through the sector for legal, moral, and religious affairs; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information went through that sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what I'm putting to you this morning is that your claims that you didn't see the civilians, the elderly people who were detained at some of the camps, that's part of the same policy, denying knowledge of civilian victims, because, as you say in your answer, everyone knew they were entitled to legal protection; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knowing that they had the right does not mean that that was denied. I'm telling that I did not know of that suffering, and this here is a general question that has to do with information about conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going turn now to a few more statements made by the media during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have first 65 ter 32585.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is an article in the "New York Times" from May of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have the end of the article in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We read that General Gvero is quoted, and we don't have it quite in the English yet. Or -- and at the very end, he says: "We say everybody has to live on his own territory. Muslims on Muslim territory, Serbs on Serbian." Says: "This is pure Serbian territory ..." And if we look two paragraphs up, we see that the area being described is the Drina valley, and they describe what had happened to the property in that area, houses blasted by tank fire, mosques reduced to rubble. First question: You were aware that your superior officer considered this area to be purely Serbian territory; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I don't know. I had no way of knowing what my superior officer was thinking. On the other hand, I don't know which territory he means. Perhaps he was in a village that was predominantly Serb. The territory of the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina, the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, is like a leopard skin, and there are differences, different ethnic groups, from one village to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what General Gvero is saying everybody has to live on his own territory, Muslims on Muslim territory, Serbs on Serbian. There were plenty of mixed villages before the war -- there were plenty of mixed territories. What he is saying is the ethnic groups in Bosnia should be separated; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to be separated. Everybody should live in his own territory, rather. And now if that territory borders on the neighbours' territory that belongs to another group, they should live one by the other. It doesn't mean that they have to be separated physically, and that was not possible after all. Most mixed marriages in the former Yugoslavia were in the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. How can you divide beds?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In fact, it's exactly what happened. Not that beds were divided but that villages that had been mixed became villages that had only one ethnicity in them; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly yes, but not in all cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 32585 receives number P7394, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7394 is admitted. Mr. Traldi, you are coming closer and closer to your 45 minutes. You're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I am. I think, with the Chamber's indulgence, I'll finish at the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's more than the 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Probably by a couple. Although, my math -- I admit my math's gotten a little bit off during the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we restarted at five minutes to 11.00. That's 45 minutes ago. I think there are a few minutes taken by the Judges. Could you conclude in the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honour. Can we have 65 ter 05716.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: 1-6. It's correct in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this isn't a statement to the press. It's an order signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic dated the 25th of April, 1995. His brigade also responsible for an area of the Drina valley. And he writes in pertinent part: "The moment has come when the issue of liberating the Serbian lands from Poturice will be finally resolved in this area by a resolute and successful action of our forces." And turning to page 2 in B/C/S, writes in pertinent part: "The adequate response of our forces meant that we realised that there would be no peace and security in Semberija and Donja Podrinje until the Poturice were completely defeated and driven out of this area." Now, this is a reflection of the same goal of separation that Gvero was expressing being turned into a document at the brigade level; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's your objection, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of separation we saw in the previous document. I think it says Muslims on Muslim territory, Serbs on Serb territory. What kind of separation we see there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see obvious facial physical separation between the Muslims who are supposed to live on the Muslim territory and the Serbs who are supposed to life on the Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that interpretation or we can see it in the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's put to the witness that this is what this document reflects and that's a proper question. The objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not provide a full answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you're welcome to do so now, sir.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I said no. This is a document of the commander of one brigade. Unfortunately, we had commanders who did not follow the positions of the Main Staff in terms of command and control and who would sometimes deviate from these positions of the Main Staff. This the first time I see this document. This the first time I hear some of these expressions, and I cannot agree that it's the same as what was quoted in one of those periodicals related to Gvero's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 5716 receives number P7395, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Mr. Traldi, I verified with Madam Registrar. It's from now that you have five minutes left, and then it's the 45 minutes. I'm strict because of this week's agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I understand and I'm very grateful to both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now the word "poturice," yes or no, as you've heard I have limited time, that refers to Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among part of the people, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have P3918.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As it comes up, sir, during the war, your salary was paid out of the 30th Personnel Centre; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you just repeat the P number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, could you answer the question, if you remember it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, your salary was paid out of the 30th Personnel Centre; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, paid as part of the assistance of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and it was my family that received my salary so that they could live at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is an article entitled: "War for a Fair Peace," published in Srpska Vojska. If we turn to page 2 in the English, still on page 1 in the B/C/S at the top of the third column, we see a reference to a speech by General Mladic, and he says in pertinent part that: "A part of our people was blinded by the idea of togetherness, brotherhood, and unity." Those are slogans from the old Communist area Yugoslavia that referred to the idea that the various ethnic groups should live together; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brotherhood and unity meant brotherhood and unity with the Slovenes too, and there were very few of them in, say, Bosnia-Herzegovina or Montenegro. So brotherhood and unity between Montenegrins and Slovenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have page 3 in the English, 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We read under the heading "Return of Unity" General Mladic pointing out as a positive in the creation of Republika Srpska and the army "the high patriotic awareness of the Serbian people" who, he says, "had headed a call to join in defence from an Ustasha invasion," and he says that "came as a result of the clearly defined goals of our struggle at the Assembly Session of Republika Srpska held on the 12th of May, 1992." First, like in the Srpska Vojska article we saw yesterday, General Mladic is saying here that the goals of the war are clear; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very small, so I couldn't finds the relevant part. However, I still stand by what I said; namely, that throughout the war there was this objective aimed at the survival of the Serb people, life in their own territory, freedom, and the establishment of lasting and permanent peace. As for this, I do apologise to you. I didn't manage to find it in the text so I barely heard what you were saying or, rather, what the interpreter was interpreting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, perhaps could the left part being enlarged. I take it it's the first column somewhere in the middle, Mr. Traldi, that you were reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It is. Just below the heading: "Return of Unity."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could that be enlarged so that the witness is better able to read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please read it? And could you also read -- a reference is made to the Assembly Session of the Republika Srpska of the 12th of May in relation to the clearly defined goals, and could you consider whether what you told us were the objectives are the ones that were clearly defined during this assembly session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I supposed to read it out loud, this text?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You could just read it for yourself and then -- because you rightly expressed your concern that you couldn't read it. Now you have read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in your previous answer you referred to goals as formulated by yourself, whereas here, in relation to the goals of the struggle, a reference is made to the Assembly Session of the Republika Srpska of the 12th of May. Those goals defined there and then, are that the same as you mentioned in your answer previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listed as at that session, no, but the essence is in what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The goals listed at that session were the strategic objectives; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And finally, sir, later in this article, and I'm just going to put the quote to you, President Karadzic is quoted, and he says this generation of Serbs in the RSK and the Republika Srpska have the duty to "save the Serbian people and once and for all avoid the danger of extermination and create a state in which there will be none of its enemies." Creating a state in which there would be none of what he termed the Serb people's enemies, that meant what General Gvero said: Serbs living on Serb territory, Muslims living on Muslim territory; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The enemy does not stand for people. The enemy is somebody who fights against the system, against the state, or something else. Here, I don't understand that as President Karadzic saying that other peoples should not live in Republika Srpska but those who fight against Republika Srpska cannot and should not live there. Those who do not recognise that authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, your time is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. We'll take break. Mr. Lukic, could you give us any indication -- but, first, we'll ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you tell us how much time you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to calculate. It's not easy. By this, I had several objections now -- that I have to clarify with the witness now. So I guess 15, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15, 20 minutes. I add to this that the Chamber has some concerns about hearing the evidence of all the witnesses this week. It's a very tight schedule, and there's perhaps an option to have some additional time on Thursday, extended session in the afternoon, but the parties are urged to see that they strictly limit themselves so that we don't have to send a witness away and then to see that witness back in four weeks from now. We take a break and will resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom. I do understand that neither party has major problems in having an extended session, if need be, on Thursday, and we are -- although we are preparing for it, of course, if we don't need it, it would be even better. In the same vein, we'll also consider whether or not to start at 9.00 on Thursday which would perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Every day to gain some time, half an hour a day, and that's before four weeks non-sitting, and it's also in the interest of your witnesses, Mr. Lukic. And, of course, you came up with a very tight schedule for this week. I'm not blaming you for it, but we have to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Although I think it's more due to long cross-examinations, not to our number of our witnesses. We brought only four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but all viva voce witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it was also intended that you perhaps discuss with Mr. Mladic a start at 9.00 exceptionally and -- for a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sokanovic, you'll now be re-examined by Mr. Lukic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Sokanovic.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Traldi said that by imposing the immediate danger of war according to the ONO law, and -- one would move from peacetime organisation into wartime organisation. Had the state of war been declared, would the civilian organs of authority also switch to wartime organisation?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, on the ground after you arrived to Bosnia and Herzegovina in late July 1992, the territory controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska, in practice, was it under a wartime organisation or did the civilian organs and the army continue to act in accordance with peacetime laws?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They acted according to peacetime laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to look at P7391 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were shown this document, the Srpska Vojska newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to look at page 2 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page here, in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And if we can go down in English version. Although it was called the second page in English, we obviously have to go to the third page in English, and it's the third paragraph from the bottom, fourth on the screen from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It states that General Milan Gvero says: "Our greatest value is the unity of the political and military leadership at all levels ..."
